title: Next year in Jerusalem
hook: long before any movement, Jewish prayer faced Jerusalem

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henrietta Szold, and your line: teach. Today a new stretch opens, with a line much older than the movement it will feed.

It's late on the first night of Passover. The matzah is crumbs, the glasses refilled again and again, and a child is asleep across two chairs. Then, at the very end of the Haggadah, the table says one line together, sometimes sung, sometimes shouted: next year in Jerusalem. The same words come back at the close of Yom Kippur, after a whole day of fasting, as the last long blast of the shofar fades. Two great nights of the Jewish year end in the same place. Not in the room. In a city.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF THE SEDER.` → `THE CLOSE OF YOM KIPPUR.` → `ENDING IN A CITY.`

segments.voice: The line rests on something Jews do every day: they pray facing Jerusalem. The roots are in the Tanakh. When Solomon dedicates the Temple, in the First Book of Kings, he asks God to hear people even when they are far away, if they pray toward the land, the city and the house. In the Book of Daniel, Daniel in Babylon goes up to his room, where the windows open toward Jerusalem, and prays there. The Talmud turns this into circles, one inside the next. Someone praying outside the land of Israel turns toward the land. Someone in the land turns toward Jerusalem. Someone in Jerusalem turns toward the Temple. Someone in the Temple turns toward its innermost room. So a whole scattered people, from every direction, leans in toward one point. The psalm of the exiles puts it as a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." So what does next year in Jerusalem mean? Jews hear it in more than one way. For some, it is a plain hope to stand in the city. For some, it waits for the days of the Messiah and a rebuilt Temple. For some, it is a picture of a world repaired. And at seders in Jerusalem itself, some people add a word: next year in Jerusalem rebuilt. Even there, the line points somewhere further. This longing came long before any political plan. In the days ahead, people answer it in very different ways.
screen: `PRAYER FACES JERUSALEM.` · `CIRCLES, ONE INSIDE THE NEXT.` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `A HOPE HEARD MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `NEXT YEAR IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: If you know which way Jerusalem lies from where you are, turn your chair or your body that way; if not, take your best guess, since the Talmud's circles are about leaning in, not about a compass. If you pray, say the psalm's line quietly, if I forget thee, O Jerusalem; if you don't, just hold the idea of one place a people has kept facing.
Jerusalem. The city Jews turn to face in prayer from everywhere in the world, the place the seder and Yom Kippur both close toward. Today's word.
Your line: leaning toward one point. The longing is old, and the answers are about to multiply. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do seders end with 'next year in Jerusalem'? Is it just a travel plan?
options: It's an old longing, said at Yom Kippur too, and Jews hear it in several ways.
It began as a slogan of the modern political movement for a Jewish state.
It's just a Passover toast, a cheerful way to close the long meal together.
